title: Beyond Scalar Rewards: Reward as a Score Distribution
hook: Human taste isn't a single number. Z-Reward models visual preference as a distribution over rubric scores, then distills that reasoning judge into a small one needing no reasoning at inference.
key_points: Visual preference is subjective; a scalar reward over-compresses uncertainty and fine score differences.
Z-Reward predicts a distribution over rubric scores, and decouples reasoning-heavy judgment from cheap reward deployment.
A large VLM teacher reasons to infer rubric-aligned score distributions, trained with Group-wise Direct Score Optimization (GDSO).
Reasoning-Internalized Score Distillation (RISD) transfers that score distribution into a compact student that needs no reasoning chains at inference.
Reported: 27B teacher 89.6% / 9B student 88.6% human-preference accuracy; used as a differentiable signal it gives ~41% net preference gain over SFT for text-to-image.
content_html: Reward models are central to post-training image generators, but visual preference is subjective — the authors argue it is better represented as a distribution over rubric scores than as one deterministic scalar. Scalar, score-token, and pairwise reward models over-compress uncertainty and small score gaps, while reasoning-based generative rewards judge well but are costly to deploy and awkward to use as a direct optimization signal. Z-Reward is a teacher–student framework that decouples the two.
extra_html: The teacher is a large VLM that reasons to infer rubric-aligned score distributions, trained with Group-wise Direct Score Optimization (GDSO) — combining policy-gradient rewards from distribution expectations with direct pointwise and pairwise supervision on score distributions and gaps. The student is trained with Reasoning-Internalized Score Distillation (RISD), inheriting the teacher's reasoning-conditioned distribution without producing explicit reasoning at inference. On the authors' annotated set, the 27B teacher reaches 89.6% human-preference accuracy and the 9B student 88.6%, closely matching the teacher while beating baselines. Used as a differentiable reward for text-to-image optimization, Z-Reward yields a reported ~41.3% net human-preference improvement over an SFT baseline.

related.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
related.hook: RLHF works but is fiddly: a separate reward model and a finicky RL loop. DPO reaches the same goal with one simple loss — and became a popular default.

related.title: InstructGPT: Aligning LMs with Human Feedback (RLHF)
related.hook: A smaller model people actually like beats a bigger one they don't. InstructGPT used human preferences to make a model follow instructions — the recipe behind ChatGPT.

flashcards.prompt: Why model a reward as a score distribution instead of a single scalar?
flashcards.back_html: Subjective preference carries uncertainty and fine-grained differences; a scalar over-compresses them, while a distribution over rubric scores preserves that structure for optimization.

flashcards.prompt: What does Reasoning-Internalized Score Distillation (RISD) give the student model?

choices.text: The teacher's reasoning-conditioned score distribution, without needing reasoning chains at inference
The ability to generate images directly

flashcards.explanation_html: RISD distills the teacher's reasoning-conditioned score distribution into a compact VLM, so the student is cheap to run yet keeps most of the teacher's judgment.

flashcards.prompt: What is the teacher–student split in Z-Reward?
flashcards.back_html: A large VLM teacher uses reasoning to infer rubric-aligned score distributions; a compact student distills that judgment for cheap, reasoning-free reward deployment.
